title: The 30-second storyboard
scenario: A tea brand wants a 30-second vertical ad. An agent drafted the storyboard in the exhibit. You decide what happens before any clip is rendered. The draft, the note and the timeline are made up for this case. The Veo lines are from Google's docs.
exhibit:
BRIEF:
  Kettle & Leaf tea. One 30-second vertical (9:16) ad on Veo 3.1.
  Clip lengths on Veo 3.1: 4, 6 or 8 seconds. Planned size: 720p unless a row says otherwise.

AGENT DRAFT (made up for this case)
  Shot  Idea                          Length  Inputs
  1     Steam rises from a kettle     8 s     text only
  2     Hands pour tea into a cup     6 s     3 reference images (cup, box, logo)
  3     Slow close-up of the cup      15 s    1080p, then extend the clip
  4     Packshot with the logo        4 s     first frame = approved packshot photo
  Agent note: "Total length: 30 seconds."

VEO 3.1 LINES (from the Google docs)
  Length must be 8 seconds with reference images, or at 1080p and 4k.
  Extension adds 7 seconds, up to 20 times, at 720p only.

TIMELINE (made up):
  The storyboard is ready Monday 10:00. Clip renders are queued for 14:00.

questions.prompt: Which rows of the draft break a Veo 3.1 rule from the exhibit?

options.text: Only row 1, because eight seconds is the longest length and the agent should have chosen less
options.explanation: Row 1 is a valid length with text only. Nothing in the Google lines forbids it.

options.text: Rows 2 and 3: reference images need 8 seconds, and an extension works at 720p only, not 1080p
options.explanation: Right. The Gemini API docs say the length must be 8 seconds with reference images, and extension works at 720p only. Row 2 has 6 seconds and row 3 asks for 1080p.

options.text: Rows 1 and 4, because a first frame and a text-only shot cannot share the same clip length
options.explanation: Rows 1 and 4 use allowed lengths, and the lines list no rule against a first frame. The trouble is in rows 2 and 3.

options.text: No row breaks a rule, because the agent wrote the draft and agents know the model's limits
options.explanation: The model only writes a plan. It can be wrong, so the plan is checked against the model's actual limits.

questions.prompt: The agent's note says the total is 30 seconds. What do you do with the draft as it stands?

options.text: Accept it, because the agent made the table itself and so its note about the table is right
options.explanation: A model can write a wrong total next to its own table. Adding takes seconds, so check it.

options.text: Accept the note and cut the last shot by 3 seconds, so that the total matches the note
options.explanation: The note is wrong, not the shot. Cutting before checking could remove a needed shot.

options.text: Ask the agent to confirm the total once more, and trust it if it says 30 a second time
options.explanation: Asking again only repeats the claim. A check by plain addition is better.

options.text: Add the lengths yourself: 8, 6, 15 and 4 make 33, so the note is wrong, and send the draft back
options.explanation: Right. The agent's total is a claim, not a sum. Anthropic's gate idea is a programmatic check, and this check is plain addition.

questions.prompt: Where should the first person's approval sit in this job?

options.text: After all four clips are rendered, so the person can judge the real pictures
options.explanation: The plan is cheap to change and the clips are not. Waiting wastes the renders.

options.text: Never, because storyboards are only for the agent and a person only sees the finished ad
options.explanation: A person can fix a wrong plan in minutes. After rendering, the same fix costs clips and credits.

options.text: After the storyboard and its checks have passed, before the render queue starts at 14:00
options.explanation: Right. This is the outline-then-check pattern: the plan is checked before the expensive step starts.

options.text: Only after the ad is posted, so that the client sees it first and the studio saves time
options.explanation: Posting is the last step. By then the studio has spent everything and the client sees the mistakes.

questions.prompt: Which check is best given to a script or a plain sum rather than to a person's taste?

options.text: Whether the story feels fresh and surprising for a young audience in the tea aisle
options.explanation: This is judgment. A person or a good reviewer decides it.

options.text: Whether the shot lengths add up to 30 and each one is a length Veo 3.1 allows
options.explanation: Right. Adding and comparing with a list gives the same answer every time, so a script or a careful sum does it.

options.text: Whether the steam in shot 1 looks warm and inviting to the client's brand manager
options.explanation: Warm and inviting is a matter of taste. It needs a person.

options.text: Whether the order of the shots tells the story the client asked for in the brief
options.explanation: Story order is a judgment call for a person who has read the brief.
